Code and data availability

The forecasting analyses were conducted using the open-source Thucia forecasting framework, available at https://github.com/kraemer-lab/Thucia. Processed data and scripts used to generate the figures and tables presented in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/kraemer-lab/pdfm-dengue-brazil. Dengue surveillance data were obtained through InfoDengue (26), with extraction and processing described in Methods; sources of climatic, demographic and environmental covariates are described in Table 1. PDFM embeddings and other data used in the study are available subject to the access and redistribution conditions of their respective providers.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Study setting, Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) representations and probabilistic forecasting framework. (A) Municipality-level cumulative reported dengue cases across Brazil from January 2010 to August 2025, shown on a log(1 + cases) scale. (B) National monthly reported dengue cases from January 2010 to August 2025, showing the January 2010-December 2019 modeltraining period and January 2020-August 2025 forecast-evaluation period. All values shown are observed case counts. (C) Pairwise Pearson correlation matrix of the 330-dimensional municipality-level PDFM embeddings. Black lines delineate the three modality-specific components of the representation: aggregated Search Trends (dimensions 0-127), Maps & Busyness (dimensions 128-255), and Weather & Air Quality (dimensions 256-329). (D) Spatial distributions of representative embedding dimensions from each PDFM component. Within each component, the displayed dimension was selected as that with the strongest absolute municipality-level correlation with an external spatial characteristic: log-transformed nighttime light intensity for Search Trends, population for Maps & Busyness, and temperature for Weather & Air Quality; the corresponding Pearson correlation coefficient (r) is shown above each map. (E) Schematic examples illustrating how the Weighted Interval Score (WIS) evaluates probabilistic forecasts. Lower WIS indicates better probabilistic forecast performance, reflecting sharper predictive distributions that remain well calibrated; higher WIS reflects wider predictive distributions and/or failure to cover the observed outcome. (F) Illustration of probabilistic forecasts at different horizons, showing observed state-level dengue cases for São Paulo from January 2019 to December 2020 and TCN forecasts fitted to the aggregated state-level case series from a common December 2019 forecast origin for target months January,

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Forecast configuration effects depend on the forecasting model. Points show the median change in Weighted Interval Score (ΔWIS) across spatial units, with vertical bars indicating the interquartile range (25th-75th percentiles). Paired forecast differences were averaged over the January 2020-August 2025 evaluation period within each municipality or state before summarising across spatial units. (A) Difference in forecast performance between models using minimal and full covariate sets (see Table 1) across 5,570 municipalities. Negative values indicate better performance with the minimal covariate set. (B) Comparison of municipality-level forecasts from models fitted independently to each municipality versus models fitted jointly across municipalities within each state, evaluated for the same 20 municipalities with the highest cumulative reported dengue case counts over the study period. Negative ΔWIS values favour independent municipality-level fitting. (C) Comparison of forecasts fitted directly to aggregated state-level case series with state-level forecasts obtained by probabilistically aggregating municipality-level

Table 1 . Epidemiological, climatic and demographic covariates used in the dengue forecasting models.

The full covariate specification included all covariates shown. The temporal specifications describe explicitly constructed covariates rather than the full historical input available to each forecasting model. Models additionally use historical dengue case sequences or autoregressive structure, as detailed in Table2. The minimal covariate specification evaluated in the covariate-selection analysis comprised log(1 + cases) at lag 1, the mean of minimum temperature over lags 1-2, and the mean of precipitation over lags 1-2.

decay: 1 × 10⁻⁵ TimesFM timesfm v1.3.0 Checkpoint: google/timesfm-2.0-500m-pytorch (updated April 2025) Architecture: 50 layers; positional embeddings Context length: 32 months Frequency mode: 1 (monthly) XReg mode: xreg + timesfm Predictive quantiles: post-hoc residual regression N-BEATS Darts v0.41.0 Input chunk length: 48 months Output chunk length: forecast horizon Dropout: 0.2 Training epochs: 150 Probabilistic fitting: quantile regression XGBoost Darts v0.41.0 / XGBoost v3.2.0 Target lags: 48 months Past-covariate lags: 48 months Output chunk length: forecast horizon Probabilistic fitting: quantile regression Estimators: 400 Maximum depth: 6 Learning rate: 0.05 Subsample: 0.9 Column sample per tree: 0.9 PDFM embeddings and residual adjustment We assessed whether Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) embeddings provided predictive information complementary to the baseline forecasting models (17). Historical PDFM embeddings aligned to individual forecast origins were not available; therefore, a single October 2023 embedding snapshot was used throughout the evaluation period. PDFM embeddings were available for 5,568 of the 5,570 municipalities included in the baseline analysis. Passabém (Minas Gerais) and Pindoba (Alagoas), were absent from the provided embeddings and so were excluded from PDFM-adjusted comparisons. To apply PDFM consistently across forecasting models, we used a residual-regression adjustment on the log(1 + cases) scale. For each forecast horizon and predictive quantile q, residuals were defined as the observed log-transformed case count minus the corresponding forecast quantile. A separate histogram-based gradient-boosting regression model with quantile (pinball) loss was fitted for each predictive quantile using municipality-level PDFM embeddings as predictors. For each target month, residual models were fitted using observations from a 24-month sliding window References
